standfirst: Three of this week's developments were not about a hazard but about the instruments the field measures hazards with. Two United Nations agencies told governments that the radio spectrum weather satellites physically depend on is being competed away; Fiji went into the pre-conference talks defending the climate panel's standing as the reference science against states that would prefer another body; and the only price yet put on Europe's lethal summer came from a credit insurer's proprietary model rather than from any journal. Against that, the sole standing United Nations machinery for climate and security turns out to have received $18.27 million in nine years, and in Nepal a flood warning that reached close to a million telephones was followed by forty-three deaths, almost all of them in landslides.
orientation:
Claims carry one of three marks. **Evidence** is what the sources actually support. **Contested** is where researchers or practitioners genuinely disagree. **Framing** is advocacy, policy narrative or institutional positioning. **Gap** is a verified absence — something looked for and not found. Sections A and D do not use the marks: A is curriculum reading, D is attributed action.

One argument runs through this week, and it is unusual enough to state plainly. This digest normally tracks *where* the climate-security argument is made: in which institution, in which register, with which vocabulary. This week the contest moved a layer down, to the apparatus that produces the facts the argument runs on.

Who certifies the science is live, because Fiji's chief negotiator says some states want bodies other than the climate panel to guide decisions (D1), and because the panel's own plenary meets on 12 October to settle whether its seventh assessment arrives in time to be used in 2028 or only in 2029. What the observing system is allowed to use is live, because the telecommunications union and the meteorological organization issued a joint appeal to protect the frequency bands that passive satellite sounding, weather radar and lightning location physically require (B2). Who prices the damage is live, because the only quantification of Europe's 2026 heat season now in circulation is an insurer's in-house damage function, and there is nothing peer-reviewed to check it against (B5). And what a warning is *for* is live, because Nepal's early-warning system performed and the people it did not save were killed by a hazard class it does not serve (B1).

Read B2, B4 and B5 against each other: three separate contests over whose number counts. Then read B1 against the Somali case this digest has been following, because the two now answer the same question — is warning the binding constraint on climate-driven loss — in opposite directions. What the week did not produce is any defence or security institution engaging any of it. The one exception is strange enough to be the most informative item here, and it is in D2.

pushback.target: This digest's own conclusion, carried for three consecutive weeks, that the field's main European convening on climate and security had quietly lapsed — and, behind that conclusion, the rule about reading institutional silence that produced it
pushback.text:
It had not lapsed. The Berlin climate and security conference is being held on 6 October 2026, hosted by the German foreign ministry with the policy institute that has run it since 2019, under the theme *A climate for security, freedom and prosperity*, in person by invitation and streamed. The nominal date reported in early September was right all along.

The error is worth more than the correction, because it was made carefully. Three weeks ago this digest split a crude rule — silence is a finding — into a better one: silence from a body with a standing publication cycle is evidence, because the schedule is the commitment, while silence from a research network between events is evidence about nothing except how long the work takes. That split was right. It was then applied to a case neither half covers.

An annual convening is neither a publication cycle nor a research network. It is a fixture, and the asymmetry of a fixture is the whole point. A host that intends to hold a conference may confirm late, may confirm only to invitees, may confirm on a microsite rather than on its publications index. A host that has cancelled one says so, because people have booked flights. For a fixture the question is therefore not whether the host has yet confirmed, but whether the host has *dis*confirmed. Non-confirmation is not evidence of cancellation; it is evidence about where a host puts announcements.

Two further things about the failure, both uncomfortable. First, the inference ran in the direction the argument wanted. A quietly dropped European convening would have been a clean instance of the trend this digest has spent six weeks documenting — climate losing its institutional vehicles while keeping its hazards — and that is precisely when a negative finding deserves more scepticism rather than less. A finding that fits is the one to re-check. Second, the non-confirmation was an artefact of looking in one place. The conference keeps its own site, separate from the institute's publications index, and three checks of that index were recorded as three pieces of evidence when they were one observation repeated three times. Repetition is not corroboration when the method is held constant.

The repair, which is now part of how this digest works: for a dated fixture, score only a disconfirmation; otherwise record that the host has not yet said, and name the page that was looked at. And when a negative finding would confirm a standing trend, go and look somewhere else before writing it down.

housekeeping:
**Three corrections to the published record.**

*Somalia.* Last week this digest said that Somalia's government and the United Nations asked for money against a near-certain flood forecast and did not get it. Money had moved one day before that sentence was written: on 24 September Britain announced £5 million for flood preparedness in Somalia, split equally between a health, nutrition, water and protection programme led by Action Against Hunger and a river-basin rehabilitation programme delivered through three agencies, expected to reach about 600,000 people against an exposed population the national disaster agency puts at 2.5 to 3.5 million. The shape of the original finding survives — the sums are small against the need, and this year's humanitarian plan remains far short — but a flat negative should not have been written on the strength of appealing agencies' statements alone. When an appeal is live, check the donors' own announcements too.

*The Security Council presidency.* Last week's note that the October presidency would pass to Switzerland, which lists climate security among its priorities, was wrong. Greece holds the October presidency.

*The European resilience framework's date.* This digest has had it as 20 October. It is 28 October. The 20th is the day the Commission presents its work programme for next year, which is a different document; the two were conflated.

**What could not be read this week.** The Dutch institute whose climate-security platform this digest tracks refused retrieval for a fourth consecutive week, so whether it published is unknown rather than negative; the platform's own separate site did open, and carries only curated work by other institutions. The energy agency's commentary on the mineral security premium would not open either, so the figures in B3 rest on the agency's own summary as reproduced by two news outlets rather than on the text; nothing load-bearing is likely to be mis-stated, but no sentence of it is quoted here for that reason. The trust fund's online dashboard for the United Nations climate-security unit again failed to render its figures, which is why B4 rests on a printed portfolio report instead — a better source, and one that should have been tried earlier. The journal archives holding this week's two curriculum texts would not open: the 1994 article was read in full from a university research group's archived copy, and the 1998 critique's nine-point structure is taken from a contemporaneous reprint rather than from the original, which the entry says.

**One sourcing note, because nothing downstream would have caught it.** The peak where this week's avalanche happened is a case where the obvious reference work misleads: the encyclopedia article under its name redirects to a neighbouring mountain about four kilometres away and a hundred metres taller. The coordinate used here comes from the structured record instead, which also carries the height given in the news coverage, and the two agree.

citation.author: Thomas F. Homer-Dixon
citation.title: Environmental Scarcities and Violent Conflict: Evidence from Cases
citation.verification_note: Author, year, venue, volume, issue and pagination all confirmed against the article's own first page, which gives International Security 19(1), Summer 1994, 5-40, published by the MIT Press. The journal archives would not open; the full text was read from a university research group's archived copy, so the summary below rests on the original rather than on secondary accounts. One detail worth recording: the citation index names the publisher as the archive rather than the MIT Press, which is an artefact of how the record was deposited.

foundational.summary:
This is the article that turned a loose 1980s claim — environmental degradation threatens security — into something testable, and the reason to read it now is that its findings are closer to the opposite of what the field remembers of it.

Homer-Dixon reports a research programme that set out three hypotheses: that falling supplies of physically controllable resources would provoke interstate 'simple-scarcity' conflicts or resource wars; that population movements caused by environmental stress would produce group-identity conflicts, especially ethnic clashes; and that severe scarcity would deepen economic deprivation and disrupt social institutions, producing civil strife and insurgency. Two case studies were built for each. The first hypothesis failed. There is, he writes, little empirical support for the claim that scarcity of renewable resources causes resource wars between states; of twelve twentieth-century conflicts over resources on Westing's list, ten concerned oil or minerals, and of the two remaining candidates one turns out to be a case of displaced peasants rather than of state competition and the other barely involved violence. What the cases supported was the quieter mechanism: diffuse, persistent, sub-national violence working through migration, economic decline and the weakening of states.

The analytical machinery is the part that survived. Scarcity has three sources — supply-induced (the resource degrades or depletes), demand-induced (more people, or more per head), and structural (the distribution of access is skewed) — and the interesting cases are the interactions. Resource capture is what happens when supply and demand pressures let powerful groups shift distribution in their favour before the shortage bites. Ecological marginalisation is what happens when demand and distribution push people onto fragile land that then degrades under them. Against these he sets ingenuity, technical and social, and the argument that social ingenuity is usually the precursor: institutions have to work before technologies can be adopted, and the countries facing the steepest scarcity are the ones with the least institutional capacity to answer it.

Two things make it live this week rather than merely formative. First, the article explicitly tells policymakers in rich countries that they give undue attention to climate change and ozone depletion, and that land, water, forest and fishery degradation will contribute more to social turmoil in the coming decades. A field that now routes almost everything through the climate referent should sit with the fact that its founding empirical text said the opposite, and ask whether it was wrong or merely early. Second, the structural-scarcity concept is the sharpest available tool for this week's own material: the question of who gets the radio spectrum, who gets the insurance, and who gets the $18.27 million is a distributional question about access, not a question about physical supply.
critiques: Gleditsch's critique is the next item and is read with it, as the sequence requires.

Case selection is the charge that has stuck hardest, and the article invites it: cases were chosen because they appeared prima facie to show a link, which Homer-Dixon frames as an attempt to falsify the null hypothesis. If the null survives in the cases most favourable to the alternative, that is informative; it still tells you nothing about base rates, and the article does not claim to.

Ingenuity has been criticised from two directions at once — as unfalsifiable, since any adaptation can be redescribed as ingenuity after the fact, and as insufficiently political, since what looks like an ingenuity deficit is often a deliberate allocation by people who benefit from the shortage. The second objection is the stronger one and the political-ecology literature of the 2000s is largely built on it.

The implications-for-security section ends in a register the article's own evidence does not reach: enfeebled states, territory seized by warlords, refugee outflows, and the alternative of 'hard' authoritarian regimes more prone to attack their neighbours. This is extrapolation, and it is the passage that policy documents quoted for twenty years while ignoring the finding that renewable-resource scarcity does not cause interstate war.

citation.author: Nils Petter Gleditsch
citation.title: Armed Conflict and the Environment: A Critique of the Literature
citation.verification_note: Author, year, venue, volume, issue and pagination confirmed against the citation index, which gives Nils Petter Gleditsch, Journal of Peace Research 35(3), May 1998, 381-400, with his affiliation at the time as the Peace Research Institute Oslo and the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. No publisher is asserted: the index's publisher field reflects the journal's current owner rather than its 1998 one. The original would not open from any route tried, so the structure of the argument below is taken from a contemporaneous reprint of its nine-point summary published alongside the Toronto group's reply, and the reply's direct quotations of it.

foundational.summary:
Gleditsch does something rarer and more useful than disagreeing with the environment-conflict thesis: he declines to argue about it and audits the research instead. The nine problems he lists are, in his order, a lack of clarity about what 'environmental conflict' even means; definitional and polemical exercises substituting for analysis; neglect of political and economic variables that both drive conflict and mediate any environmental influence; models grown so large and complex as to be virtually untestable; selection of cases on values of the dependent variable; reversed causality; postulated future events cited as empirical evidence; failure to distinguish foreign from domestic conflict; and confusion about the appropriate level of analysis. He is explicit that no single publication has all nine, and that many have several.

The force of the list is that most of the items are not about the environment at all. They are the standard apparatus of quantitative social science applied to a literature that had grown up outside it, and the implicit charge is that a field with policy traction had acquired it without passing the tests any other conflict literature would have had to pass. That is why the piece became the hinge of the field: it redirected a generation of work from case studies toward large-N designs with specified controls, and the entire second empirical wave — up to and including the climate-conflict econometrics of the 2010s and the methodological scepticism that still polices it — runs downstream of it.

The Toronto group's published reply, read here in the same sitting, is as instructive as the critique. It concedes nothing on the central conceptual point and attacks the premise: Gleditsch's preferred distinction between 'simple resource scarcity' and 'environmental degradation' is, they argue, unworkable, because degradation is only one of two ways supply falls (the other is depletion), and because a resource's absolute supply is not the causally interesting quantity in the first place. What matters is supply relative to demand and relative to the social distribution of access — which is exactly why the Homer-Dixon definition folds all three in. Their broader charge is that the quasi-experimental standard Gleditsch applies is a methodological straitjacket that would discard the detailed findings of every case-based project in the field, including those he does not actually engage with.

Read as a pair, the exchange is the field's foundational argument about evidence, and neither side won it outright. Gleditsch's list of defects was adopted almost wholesale. His definitional proposal was not, and the integrated conception of scarcity he objected to is the one the field still uses.
critiques: The reply's strongest point is that the critique treats a heterogeneous literature with a single brush, associating the more rigorous projects with the least rigorous and then declining to test the specific findings of either.

The methodological objection cuts both ways and the subsequent thirty years show it. The large-N turn Gleditsch called for delivered real discipline and also a durable problem of its own: aggregate designs that find small or null average effects are poor instruments for mechanisms that are local, lagged and distributional, which is what the case literature was trying to describe.

Point seven — postulated future events cited as empirical evidence — is the one the field has never fixed, and it is worth carrying into the rest of this digest. Scenario output, modelled projections and proprietary damage functions all now circulate as findings; B5 is an instance in this very week's material.

citation.author: Tobias Böhmelt and Zorzeta Bakaki
citation.title: Peace treaties' environmental provisions and conflict recurrence
citation.verification_note: Authors, title, venue, volume, issue, pagination and dates confirmed against the citation index: Tobias Böhmelt and Zorzeta Bakaki, both University of Essex, Environment and Security 4(3), 249-269, published online 24 January 2026 and in the September 2026 issue. The abstract was read in the publisher's own deposited record; the full text was not opened, so the account below describes the design and the stated finding and does not interrogate the specification.

foundational.summary:
Chosen deliberately as the pair to this week's curriculum reading, because it asks the Homer-Dixon question from the far end. The 1994 article asked whether environmental scarcity helps cause conflict; this asks whether environmental cooperation helps end it, and it does so with exactly the design Gleditsch spent 1998 demanding.

Böhmelt and Bakaki code provisions for environmental cooperation across more than a thousand peace treaties concluded since the end of the Cold War and test them against conflict recurrence. The central finding is that environmental clauses are associated with a significantly lower risk of renewed conflict. Their claim about what this means is carefully pitched: not that the environment is the engine of peace, but that environmental provisions are not merely symbolic — that they do substantive work in post-conflict settlement rather than functioning as decorative language added late in a negotiation.

Why it belongs in this week's reading. The environmental peacebuilding thesis has been asserted for roughly three decades on a handful of cases and a great deal of advocacy, and it occupies a position in the policy architecture out of all proportion to its evidence: the United Nations climate-security machinery in B4, the peacekeeping advisers it deploys, and most climate-peace programming all rest on some version of it. A cross-national test of it is therefore the kind of result that ought to change how an institution argues for its budget. It also shows how much the field's evidentiary standard has moved since 1994. Homer-Dixon's six paired case studies were state of the art in their decade; this study's thousand treaties are unremarkable in theirs. Whether the gain in external validity cost anything in understanding of mechanism is the standing question of the whole phase, and it is the right one to carry forward.

Treat the finding as a promising association, not a settled causal claim. The obvious selection problem is that the negotiators who put environmental cooperation into a treaty may be the ones negotiating the settlements most likely to hold for other reasons; which is, almost word for word, Gleditsch's third and sixth points, turned around and pointed at the optimistic side of the literature.
critiques: Endogeneity is the first thing to ask of it: treaties with environmental provisions may be longer, more detailed and more internationally supervised than those without, and treaty depth is itself a known predictor of durability. Whether the specification separates the clause from the context cannot be assessed from the abstract alone.

'Environmental provisions' is a broad coding category, spanning everything from a shared river commission to a line about natural-resource revenue sharing. The policy question — which kind of provision does the work — is the one a binary indicator cannot answer.

The venue is the field's own young journal rather than a general conflict journal, which is worth noting for a result that supports the field's central practical claim. That is not an objection to the work; it is a reason to want it replicated somewhere with a sceptical readership.

developments.title: Nepal's warning system reached a million telephones and forty-three people died anyway
developments.place: Baglung, Manang, Myagdi and Mustang districts, Nepal
developments.body:
A low-pressure system over the Bay of Bengal put more than 100 millimetres of rain across 186 monitoring stations in Nepal between 24 and 27 September, with peaks of 544.2 millimetres at Dedhgaun, 500.2 at Panchase and 472 at Atraulitar. The national disaster authority recorded 542 rain-related incidents over those four days: 304 landslides, which killed 20 people, and 87 floods, which killed four. By 1 October the combined toll from the week's rain-related events had reached at least 43. Separately, on 27 September an avalanche struck the base camp on Himlung Himal in Manang, where 16 expedition support workers were reported missing; 11 bodies had been recovered by 1 October and five were still unaccounted for, with at least ten people rescued from the mountain. Landslides dammed rivers in Manang and Mustang, creating downstream flood risk; 227 houses were destroyed, 142 damaged and 31 bridges damaged.

The number to hold onto is a different one. The authority sent flood-warning text messages to approximately 980,000 people and 2,000 were evacuated, with helicopter rescues from Myagdi, Jajarkot and Baglung. By any reasonable standard the warning system worked: it had lead time, it reached a population the size of a European capital, and it moved people. Almost everyone who died was killed by a landslide, which is the hazard class that system does not and largely cannot serve — lead times of seconds to minutes, locations not knowable in advance, and no evacuation geography to send anyone to.
developments.arc_note: The fifth consecutive week in which the Himalayan hazard file has produced a new finding, and the second in which the finding is about the limits of warning rather than about the event. The trend this digest has been tracking — high-mountain hazard migrating from the mode monitoring was built for to the mode it was not — now has a third mode in it. August's rock-ice cascade was too fast to warn against. This week's riverine flooding was warned against successfully. The landslides in between are the category where the hazard is slow enough to forecast in aggregate and far too local to forecast in particular, and that is where the bodies were.

attribution.note: No event attribution study of this episode exists, and none was announced. The attribution network that published on the Himalayan cascade on 17 September has published nothing since and nothing on this. Its finding then — roughly 1.5°C of warming on July-August temperatures in the region, about 2°C annually, and the freezing level rising about 100 metres per decade — is the nearest thing to a hazard-environment attribution available for these slopes, and it is about the hazard environment rather than about any particular slope failure. The honest statement is that the regional hazard environment is attributed and this week's 304 landslides are not.

claims.text: The national disaster authority recorded 542 rain-related incidents between 24 and 27 September, including 304 landslides that killed 20 people and 87 floods that killed four, with 227 houses destroyed and 31 bridges damaged. By 1 October the combined toll across all of the week's events had reached at least 43, with five avalanche victims still missing.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The avalanche on Himlung Himal on 27 September hit a base camp holding expedition support workers. Sixteen were reported missing; two deaths were confirmed within a day, and the recovered toll reached 11 by 1 October.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No security institution engaged any of it. Nothing was found from the regional organisations, from any defence ministry, or from the three-country mechanism Nepal proposed from the General Assembly rostrum six days earlier, whose stated purposes include joint early warning and coordinated cross-border relief. The week's events are exactly the case that proposal was written for, and neither India nor China has responded to it.

claims.label: contested
claims.text: Whether early warning is the binding constraint on climate-driven humanitarian loss now has two dated answers pointing opposite ways, and they are not reconcilable by splitting the difference. In Somalia the warning is months ahead, the measures are specified, and the constraint is money. Here the warning arrived, the money was not the issue, and the constraint was the hazard's physics. Practitioners who argue the question in general terms — on either side — are arguing about an average that does not exist. The operational question is which hazard class, in which terrain, with what lead time, and the field does not currently ask it that way.

nl_eu.note: No Dutch or European link worth asserting. It matters because it is the sharpest available correction to a premise that European adaptation and development policy rests on heavily: that strengthening early warning is the highest-return intervention available. For riverine flooding on this evidence it is. For slope failure it is not, and the European instrument now in preparation for 28 October identifies vulnerable territories and will have to decide whether its risk owners are accountable for hazards that cannot be warned against.

developments.title: Two UN agencies tell governments the observing system's radio spectrum is being competed away
developments.body:
At the opening of a global seminar on spectrum use for meteorology, held at ITU headquarters in Geneva from 28 to 30 September, the Secretaries-General of the ITU and the WMO issued a joint appeal to governments, regulators and meteorological services to protect the radio-frequency bands that weather and climate observation depends on. The systems they name are the backbone of the entire warning and attribution apparatus: satellite sensors that measure naturally occurring atmospheric signals, weather radar, lightning location systems, aircraft and marine observations, and hydrological monitoring. Doreen Bogdan-Martin said that preventing harmful radio interference is a matter of public safety and can save lives, and that interference-free spectrum keeps forecasts accurate, alerts timely and climate data reliable. Celeste Saulo put the structural point: the spectrum is a finite natural resource, and meteorology relies on specific bands determined not by choice but by the physical properties of the atmosphere itself. The seminar reviewed recent and forthcoming spectrum decisions ahead of the 2027 World Radiocommunication Conference.

Saulo's sentence is the one that makes this a security story rather than a technical one. Most contested resources can be substituted at a price. Passive microwave sounding cannot: the frequencies at which water vapour and oxygen emit are set by molecular physics, so a band reallocated to a commercial service is not a band meteorology can trade out of. The asymmetry that follows is brutal. Mobile and satellite broadband operators arrive at a spectrum conference with revenue, national champions and ministries of economy behind them; the observing system arrives with a public good that has no price attached and no constituency that notices its degradation until a forecast fails.
developments.arc_note: Novel in this digest and, as far as can be established, novel as a framing from these two institutions jointly. Spectrum allocation for meteorology has been contested at every radiocommunication conference since the 2000s and is normally fought inside the technical committees. What is new is the escalation out of that forum into a public joint appeal by both Secretaries-General, framed in the language of public safety and lives, nineteen months before the conference that will decide. That is what an institution does when it expects to lose on the technical merits.

attribution.note: No event. The observable is institutional behaviour, and the appeal's own framing is about future capability rather than past damage.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The ITU and WMO Secretaries-General issued a joint appeal on 28 September to protect meteorological radio spectrum, naming satellite sensors, weather radar, lightning location, aircraft and marine observations and hydrological monitoring as dependent systems, and pointing to the 2027 World Radiocommunication Conference.

source.title: ITU and WMO call to protect radio spectrum for weather, climate and water services

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Saulo's formulation is that meteorology's bands are 'determined not by choice, but by the physical properties of the atmosphere itself'. This is the technical reason the resource is not substitutable and therefore not tradable, which is unlike almost every other contested input in this field.

source.title: ITU and WMO call to protect radio spectrum for weather, climate and water services

claims.label: framing
claims.text: 'A matter of public safety' is a deliberate register shift. It moves spectrum from a question of economic regulation, where meteorology has no leverage, to a question of civil protection, where it has some. It is the same operation the climate field has performed on defence vocabulary for two decades, running in the opposite direction, and it is worth watching whether it works any better here.

source.title: ITU and WMO call to protect radio spectrum for weather, climate and water services

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No defence or security institution has engaged the question in anything found this week, which is the oddity. Military meteorology depends on the same bands, allied early warning depends on the same satellites, and the alliance resilience requirements revised on 15 September name space weather and changing environmental conditions among cross-cutting risks without anywhere identifying the observing system those assessments are built on as an asset to be defended.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No figure was found, from either agency or from any national regulator, for how much of the protected meteorological spectrum is actually under live reallocation pressure in the 2027 conference agenda. Without that the appeal cannot be weighed: it is impossible to tell from the public record whether this is a marginal defensive action or an existential one.

nl_eu.note: European states are on both sides of this inside their own administrations: the same ministries that fund the meteorological services and the European satellite programmes also run the spectrum auctions that fund their treasuries, and they coordinate a single negotiating position for the radiocommunication conference through the European conference of postal and telecommunications administrations. The Dutch case is the type instance, with a meteorological institute that is part of the attribution community and a telecommunications authority with a strong auction record. Which of the two wins inside each administration is a concrete, checkable test of how seriously European governments treat the evidence base they keep citing.

developments.title: The energy agency prices security itself: diversification as an insurance premium
developments.body:
In a commentary published on 30 September, Shobhan Dhir and Tae-Yoon Kim of the IEA proposed that the extra cost of diversifying critical-mineral supply away from concentrated sources be understood and named as a 'mineral security premium' — an insurance policy against supply disruption rather than a competitiveness penalty to be minimised. The arithmetic behind the proposal is the argument. The agency estimates that full implementation of China's October 2025 expansion of export controls could put about $6.5 trillion of annual sales at risk across the energy, automotive, electronics and defence sectors outside China, while the annual market for magnet rare earths themselves is under $10 billion. On the cost side, critical minerals account for roughly a quarter of battery cell costs but about 3 per cent of the price of an average electric vehicle, and rare earths for around 40 per cent of permanent magnet costs but under 1 per cent of a car's value. The premium, in other words, is payable on a small base against an exposure three orders of magnitude larger.

Two things make this more than a minerals story. First, defence is named as one of the four exposed sectors by an energy agency writing about transition inputs, which is the energy-security and climate-security arguments arriving at the same sentence from opposite directions. Second, and more interesting, the move is conceptual: it converts a security argument into a priced option. For twenty years this field's problem has been that security framing buys attention but not budget, because the threat is diffuse and the counterfactual unmeasurable. An insurance premium has neither problem. It has a number, a payer and a renewal date, and it does not require anyone to agree about the probability of the disruption to agree about the price of the cover.
developments.arc_note: An acceleration of the substitution trend this digest has tracked since week one, in which climate and transition arguments migrate into whichever security register is locally unoccupied — economic security at the European Parliament, energy supply security at Climate Week, raw-materials security in Dutch development-cooperation research. This is the furthest that migration has gone: not into another security register but out of the security register altogether, into insurance. Note what is gained and lost. Insurance language is commensurable with budgets in a way threat language is not. It also strips out everything about the harm that cannot be priced, which is most of what the human-security half of this field is about.

claims.text: The agency's estimate is that full implementation of the October 2025 export-control expansion could put about $6.5 trillion of annual sales at risk across energy, automotive, electronics and defence sectors outside China, against an annual market for magnet rare earths of under $10 billion.

source.title: Global critical mineral concentration and export controls puts USD 6.5 trillion industry outside China at risk: IEA

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The cost-side figures are the argument's load-bearing part: critical minerals at roughly a quarter of battery cell costs but about 3 per cent of an average electric vehicle's price, and rare earths at around 40 per cent of permanent magnet costs but under 1 per cent of a car's value.

source.title: A price worth paying? A mineral security premium as insurance against supply disruptions

claims.label: framing
claims.text: 'A security premium that provides insurance against the risks associated with concentration' is the agency's own formulation, and it is advocacy as much as analysis: the agency has argued for diversification for five years and has now found a vocabulary in which the cost of its preferred policy reads as prudence rather than as protectionism. That it is advocacy does not make it wrong, and the ratio it rests on is unusually robust to the choice of assumptions.

developments.title: The UN's only standing climate-security machinery has received $18.27 million in nine years
developments.date: Figure covers 2016 to 2024; established this week
developments.place: United Nations Multi-Partner Trust Fund Office, New York
developments.body:
This digest has carried a question about the funding of the joint United Nations climate-security unit open since its first week, and has twice reported that the online dashboard would not render its figures. It still will not. A printed portfolio report does, and the number is now on the record: cumulative deposits to the joint programme between 2016 and 2024 were $18.27 million.

That figure means little alone and a great deal in its own table. The report ranks fifteen funds in the office's climate and environment portfolio by cumulative deposits over the same period. The forest initiative at the top has taken $808.89 million. A single-country local-government climate initiative has taken $27.23 million. A humanitarian-energy fund has taken $22.21 million. The climate-security unit sits thirteenth of fifteen, below both, at a little over 2 per cent of the largest fund and about $2 million a year. It is supported by fourteen contributing governments and runs, per its own pages, a third phase from 2026 to 2028 with ten advisers deployed to missions and regional organisations — most recently a climate, peace and security adviser to the Pacific Islands Forum, onboarded in June 2026 at Pacific states' request.

Two consequences follow and both change how this digest reads the field. The first is arithmetic: Britain's £1 million of 25 September, which this digest reported as three tenths of one per cent of a £331 million package and treated as a rounding error, is on the order of 5 per cent of everything this programme has ever received. The denominator was wrong. A single million pounds is a material contribution to the machinery, which is a statement about the machinery rather than about the generosity. The second is structural. The field has spent six weeks of this digest asking whether security institutions will adopt the climate referent. The institution that already has one is funded at about the level of a mid-sized national research grant, and almost all of its money comes from the same small group of European and Commonwealth states that already agree with it.
developments.arc_note: Corrects this digest's own framing twice over: the funding question is answered in magnitude, and the reading of the British contribution as negligible was an artefact of comparing it to the wrong total. The underlying trend — institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment — is confirmed and relocated. This digest has been tracking that pattern in the Dutch state and treating it as a Dutch peculiarity. It is also true of the multilateral system's own climate-security instrument, which suggests the pattern is about what this policy area attracts rather than about any particular government.

developments.title: Europe's lethal summer gets its first price, and it comes from a credit insurer's model
developments.date: 24 September 2026, in wide circulation through this week
developments.body:
The only quantification now circulating of what Europe's 2026 heat season cost is an insurer's. Allianz published its first annual climate economics report on 24 September, estimating the 2026 heatwaves at about €113 billion of annual output across 30 European countries, or roughly 0.46 per cent of their combined projected output, with Italy, Germany and France accounting for nearly two-thirds and Cyprus taking the largest proportional hit at 1.74 percentage points of growth. The method uses each country's most intense five-day heat episode between June and August, adjusted for humidity and population exposure. The same report puts a developing strong El Niño at about $451 billion globally, concentrated in 2027, with China, the United States and India carrying roughly 60 per cent of gross losses at $147 billion, $91 billion and $50 billion. The figures were picked up widely in the first days of October, including in the Indian business press on 2 October, which is when they entered general circulation.

Nothing here is obviously wrong, and that is the problem. The estimates come from a proprietary platform combining climate data with the firm's own damage functions, explicitly designed to capture losses beyond insurance claims. They are not peer-reviewed, they cannot be replicated from the public record, and they are produced by a company whose business is selling cover against the thing being measured. They will nonetheless be the number in every European policy document for a year, because there is no other number. This is Gleditsch's seventh problem — postulated events cited as empirical evidence — arriving twenty-eight years later with better graphics, and it is also the exact slot the European framework due on 28 October will have to fill when it starts assigning risk owners and standing up an insurance alliance.
developments.arc_note: A repeat of a pattern this digest flagged in week three, when a modelled figure of €180 billion of lost European output from a bank's heat study was carried into a parliamentary intervention by the climate convention's own executive secretary as though it were research. Same structure, bigger institution, wider circulation. The pattern is that the field's most quotable numbers about climate damage in Europe are now produced by financial firms rather than by public science, because public science is slower and will not estimate what it cannot bound.

attribution.note: The report attributes economic losses to heat episodes; it does not claim, and should not be read as claiming, an attribution of those episodes to climate change. No event attribution study of the 2026 European heat season was found. The attribution network published on European marine heat on 19 August and has published nothing since. So the causal chain that policy will treat as established — warming caused the heat, the heat cost €113 billion — has an unattributed first link and an unreviewed second one.

developments.title: The Security Council's October has no climate item, and the succession is the month's business
developments.body:
Greece took the Council presidency for October and set out its programme of work at a press conference on 1 October. Its President for the month, Aglaia Balta, announced two signature events: a briefing on children and armed conflict on 26 October, marking the mandate's thirtieth anniversary and chaired by the Greek foreign minister, and a high-level debate on emerging technologies with an emphasis on maritime security on 29 October, chaired by the Greek prime minister. The rest of the month carries a Middle East debate on 15 October, a women, peace and security debate on 27 October, and a seminar and consultative meeting with the African Union on 21 to 23 October. Climate is not on the programme in any form.

What the presidency did name as the month's real business is the succession. October, Balta said, is the month to make progress on or even agree the next Secretary-General, with several straw polls planned, and the presidency would try to facilitate consensus in the Council while remaining available to the wider membership. The fourth straw poll had already been held on 29 September, with seven candidates after Michelle Bachelet's withdrawal on 20 September. The Council did not release results; reporting gives Rebeca Grynspan at ten encourage, three discourage and two no opinion — up one encourage and down two discourage on the third poll — and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett at eight and six. The Council has still not moved to colour-coded ballots, which is the step that would reveal whether the discouragement sits with a permanent member.
developments.arc_note: The sixth consecutive week in which the Council has produced nothing on climate, and the clearest instance yet of the shift this digest has tracked from climate security toward natural-resource governance and then toward nothing at all. Worth noting what did get a signature event: emerging technologies with a maritime emphasis. A Council that will convene its prime minister for the security implications of technological change at sea, and will not convene anyone for the security implications of the sea itself, has made a choice about which novel risk is sayable in that room.

developments.title: Europe's climate resilience framework is fixed for 28 October, with an insurance alliance and no supply security
developments.date: Through this week; presentation set for 28 October 2026
developments.body:
The most consequential pending instrument in this digest now has a firm date and a clearer shape. The Commission will present its integrated framework for climate resilience on 28 October: a communication, a legislative proposal, a recommendation addressed to both public and private sectors, and a Commission decision. Its announced contents include the identification of Europe's hundred most vulnerable territories, a 3°C reference scenario for Europe in the legislative proposal, a duty on the Union and member states to assign named risk owners for every major climate risk in key sectors, a climate insurance alliance, and a European heatwave plan. The Environment Council meets on 12 October, before the presentation, with emissions trading reform and the November conference on its agenda; the Energy Council meets on 29 October, the day after.

One thing about it is worth a closer look than it will get. A specialist European policy service reported this week that the framework remains due on 28 October and that security of supply goes unmentioned in it. The body of that report could not be opened, so the finding rests on its headline and is recorded as such — but it is consistent with everything else visible about the instrument. The Commission's own page frames the framework as safeguarding Europe's security and prosperity in a sense that is economic and social rather than strategic, and the announced architecture is about risk ownership, insurance and vulnerable territories rather than about continuity of supply under stress. That is a notable divergence from where the alliance went on 15 September, when its revised resilience requirements obliged allies to hold exercised contingency plans to secure food and water supply during crisis and conflict. Two European resilience instruments, six weeks apart, one defining resilience as insured recovery and the other as assured supply.
developments.arc_note: An acceleration of the European resilience track, and a sharpening of the decoupling this digest named last week. The alliance kept the hazards and dropped the word climate; the Union is keeping the word climate and, on the available evidence, dropping the supply-security content. Each institution is building the half of resilience its own competence allows, and nothing visible connects the two halves.

nl_eu.note: As direct as it gets, and the Dutch stake is unusually concrete. A duty to name a risk owner for every major climate risk cuts straight across the Dutch delta governance model, which distributes responsibility between a commissioner, water authorities, provinces and municipalities by design rather than by accident. A European obligation to name one accountable owner per risk is either a vindication of the Dutch commissioner model or a challenge to its diffuseness, and which of the two it turns out to be will be legible in the Dutch government's first reaction after 28 October.

moves.title: Fiji sets the pre-conference terms and defends the climate panel as the reference body
moves.actor: Dr Sivendra Michael, Permanent Secretary for Environment and Climate Change and chief negotiator, Fiji
moves.body: Six days before hosting the pre-conference talks, Fiji's permanent secretary and chief negotiator set out publicly the four positions Fiji would carry into them: hold the line on science and 1.5°C, climate finance, oceans, and Pacific leadership. The first of the four is the one that matters analytically, because of the reason he gave for it. The science position was under threat, he said, because some countries want scientific bodies other than the climate panel to guide decisions — and his objection was procedural rather than scientific: 'That limits participation of small countries like Pacific because we don't have such kind of scientific bodies like a NASA.' He cited the International Court of Justice's treatment of the panel as the authoritative science, and added, on finance, that it should not take eighteen months to disburse a fund when a community is waiting another eighteen. Over 1,800 people had registered for the public programme and 550 for the negotiating zone. The talks opened on 5 October in Nadi, with Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya carrying three messages — keep 1.5°C within reach, make finance reach communities, give the ocean its place in the climate regime — and with Australia's climate minister presiding over negotiations for the November conference.
moves.stated_rationale: Keeping 1.5°C within reach, protecting access to finance, and securing the ocean's standing in the climate regime, with Pacific leadership of the agenda as the fourth pillar. On the science question specifically: that substituting other scientific bodies for the panel would exclude states without large national research agencies from the decisions those bodies would inform.
moves.inference: This is a procedural defence of an evidentiary monopoly, and it is the shrewdest move in this week's digest. The small-island negotiating position has rested for a decade on 1.5°C retaining the character of a commitment, and every attempt to defend that character substantively — against overshoot findings, against the physics — has lost ground. Michael is not defending the number. He is defending the institution that certifies the number, on grounds of participation rather than of accuracy, and participation is a claim small states can win where accuracy is a claim they cannot. If the reference body changes, the assessment changes, and the legal and financial entitlements built on the assessment change with it; the ocean pillar and the sea-level declaration adopted five days earlier in New York depend on the same chain. Read alongside the reported resistance of five states to the earlier of two timetables for the panel's next assessment, this suggests the fight over the climate panel's standing has moved from a fringe position to a live negotiating issue on two axes simultaneously, and it will be decided at the panel's own plenary from 12 October rather than at the conference in November.

moves.title: The American climate-security institute takes the frame to Arctic solar geoengineering
moves.actor: Center for Climate and Security, Council on Strategic Risks, with Reflective
moves.body: On 2 October the Center for Climate and Security announced a private, in-person tabletop exercise with the solar-geoengineering research organisation Reflective, to be held on 14 October alongside the Montréal climate security summit. The scenario is a fictional 2030 deployment of stratospheric aerosol injection designed to slow rising Arctic surface temperatures; participants are to weigh geopolitical implications and debate the security risks, trade-offs and uncertainties of such an intervention, with particular attention to how different deployment approaches would affect sea ice. No prior expertise is required and no participants are named. The summit it sits alongside, on 15 and 16 October, is convened by the alliance's climate change and security centre of excellence with a Canadian defence association under the title 'Resilient Defence: Climate-Smart Investments on the Road to 5%', with nine thematic tracks including procurement resilience metrics, climate intelligence in planning, critical-minerals supply chains and operational energy, and a speaker list of serving officers and ambassadors. It is by invitation.
moves.stated_rationale: To examine the security dynamics of a proposed climate intervention at high latitudes: the geopolitical implications, the security risks, the trade-offs and the uncertainties, including the effect of different deployment designs on sea ice.
moves.inference:
Three things, in ascending order of consequence. First, the institute is doing what institutes do when their customer closes: this digest has spent three weeks watching it write for statehouses, and this week it is running a great-power scenario exercise on a technology no state has deployed. Those are not the same strategy, and the state-level relocation now looks less like a durable repositioning than one of several simultaneous bets.

Second, the venue choice is the real move. A tabletop produces no citable document, has no named participants and leaves no record anyone can dispute, which makes it exactly the instrument for introducing a subject too radioactive to publish on. Solar radiation modification governance is where the institute's director turned her own writing in May 2026, and this digest flagged that then as an early indicator of where the security frame travels next. It has travelled, and it has travelled into a format designed not to be quotable.

Third, and this is the part worth arguing with: a security exercise about Arctic aerosol injection is being run before any security institution has published an assessment of Arctic aerosol injection, and the exercise's own framing concerns how deployment designs affect sea ice — a question of physical efficacy that a geopolitical tabletop is not equipped to answer and that the research organisation co-convening it has a direct interest in. Whether the format is being used to surface risks or to normalise the premise cannot be determined from outside, and the absence of participants and outputs means it will not be determinable afterwards either. That opacity is itself the finding: the field's most consequential emerging question is being worked in a room with no minutes.

moves.title: Greece's Council presidency builds an October with no climate in it
moves.actor: Aglaia Balta, President of the Security Council for October 2026, for Greece
moves.body: A Council presidency's programme of work is one of the few genuinely discretionary acts in the institution, and Greece used its month on two signature events: children and armed conflict on 26 October, at the thirtieth anniversary of the mandate and chaired by its foreign minister, and emerging technologies with an emphasis on maritime security on 29 October, chaired by its prime minister. Around them sit a Middle East debate, a women, peace and security debate, and a seminar and consultative meeting with the African Union. Climate appears nowhere. Setting out the programme, Balta named the succession as the month's substantive business, with several straw polls planned and an explicit aim of agreement inside October, and said the presidency would try to facilitate consensus in the Council while remaining available to the wider membership.
moves.stated_rationale: Two thematic priorities — the protection of children in armed conflict at a mandate anniversary, and the security implications of emerging technologies with a maritime emphasis — alongside the Council's standing files and the facilitation of the Secretary-General's selection.
moves.inference: A choice, not an omission, and the most informative thing about it is which novel risk was selected. Greece is a maritime state with the largest merchant fleet in the world and an acute interest in the sea; it gave its prime minister's time to technological change at sea and nothing to the sea itself. Compare it with the alternative that was available. A week before the programme was announced, the General Assembly had adopted by consensus the first United Nations declaration on sea-level rise, settling as state practice that statehood and maritime entitlements survive the physical loss of territory — a first-order question about sovereignty, exclusive economic zones and the law of the sea, which is Council business by any reading, carried by a text no state opposed. A maritime presidency declined to pick it up. The thread this digest opened last week — whether any security institution would read the declaration as a security instrument — has its first answer, and it is the strongest available negative: not that nobody noticed, but that the institution best placed to act had the opportunity, the competence and the national interest, and used its month on something else.

moves.title: Berlin's climate-security conference is held after all, under the theme of security, freedom and prosperity
moves.actor: The German Federal Foreign Office with adelphi
moves.body:
The annual Berlin climate and security conference, held since 2019 and the field's principal European convening, takes place on 6 October 2026 under the theme 'A climate for security, freedom and prosperity'. It is hosted by the German foreign ministry with the policy institute that founded it, in person by invitation and streamed, with stated objectives of accelerating climate-security integration across sectors, building cross-sectoral coalitions, generating policy recommendations and demonstrating that national and human security have to be considered together. Side events and strategic meetings are scheduled with the climate for peace initiative and the climate security expert network.

It is recorded as a move for two reasons, one of them about this digest. A foreign ministry keeping the field's flagship convening alive in a year when the field's institutional vehicles have been closing is a deliberate act with a cost attached, and the theme's three nouns are a choice: 'security, freedom and prosperity' is the vocabulary of a German foreign policy arguing for climate inside a coalition that does not lead with climate, which is the same substitution operation this digest has tracked in four other capitals. The second reason is that this digest concluded for three consecutive weeks that the 2026 edition was not happening, on the strength of its absence from the institute's publications index. That was wrong, and why it was wrong is in the pushback above. The date falls two days after this week closes and is recorded now rather than next week precisely because the correction should not wait.
moves.stated_rationale: To accelerate the integration of climate security across diplomacy, defence and development; to build cross-sectoral coalitions; to generate actionable policy recommendations; and to demonstrate that national and human security must be considered together.
moves.inference: The last of those four objectives is the one to test the proceedings against. 'National and human security must be considered together' is the field's own founding claim and the thing it has been losing: the two halves have been coming apart all year, with national security keeping the hazards and shedding the climate referent while human security keeps the referent and sheds the budget. A convening that states the integration as an objective is implicitly conceding it has broken. What to watch is not the speeches but whether anything with a named owner comes out: the conference has no standing output document, which is why six previous editions have produced influence that is impossible to trace. In-person by invitation, with the stream as the public record, is also a format choice worth noting in the same week as an unminuted tabletop in Washington (D2).

roster_silences:
**Silent, and by the split rule this matters.** The international military council on climate and security published nothing, for a fifth consecutive week. Its most recent item of any kind remains an open letter of 23 October 2025 arguing for clean energy investment inside the alliance's 1.5-per-cent non-core defence spending target, and there has been no world climate and security report since the 2024 edition. The dormancy is now worth more than a tally, because this week supplied the test it fails: a defence-climate summit convened by the alliance's own centre of excellence under the title 'Resilient Defence: Climate-Smart Investments on the Road to 5%' is, almost exactly, the argument the council made a year ago and then stopped making. A body with a named chair, a named secretary general and a standing report series has gone silent in the month its position became other people's agenda.

**Silent, and this is only lead time.** The attribution network has published nothing since 17 September and nothing on Europe's heat season or Nepal's landslides. Under the rule corrected in week four, absence of output from a research network between events is evidence about how long the work takes and nothing else; the question to ask of it is whether it has declined a case it was asked to take, and nothing suggests it has. The same applies to the Stockholm institute, whose climate-change-and-security publications list still ends at the August study on Abyei with nothing for September, and to the mountain centre in Kathmandu, which published nothing on this week's events in its own region.

**Unknown, which is a third category and not a finding.** The Dutch institute refused retrieval for a fourth consecutive week. Four refusals means its silence cannot be assessed at all, and the standing instruction — stop retrying the domain, go to the sister site — was followed: the platform's own site opened and carries curated work by others, including a piece arguing that the Security Council is deadlocked on climate and that incoming members have a route forward, which this week's October programme does not bear out.

**Not silent, and nobody had been looking.** The Berlin institute's conference is on 6 October (D4), which this digest had written off. And the African Union's peace and security council met at ministerial level on 23 September on regional responses to security and terrorism challenges, naming the adverse impacts of climate change among the transnational challenges it is concerned by, with a joint task force meeting with the United Nations on 26 September — both just before this window opened and neither carried into it. The Union produced nothing in the window itself, which given that the Council's October programme includes a two-day seminar with it on 21 and 22 October is a lead-time absence rather than an informative one.

watch.title: Whether the pre-conference talks settle the climate panel's standing or defer it
watch.note: The talks run 5 to 8 October in Nadi with a limited delegation continuing to Tuvalu, with about 4,000 participants from 60 countries reported and fewer than a dozen leaders confirmed. Three things have datable answers by the close. Whether the outcome text or the chair's summary names the climate panel as the reference science, which is the specific thing Fiji's chief negotiator says is under threat. Whether the ocean roadmap Fiji is seeking acquires any named deliverable for the November conference. And whether the sea-level declaration adopted in New York on 24 September is cited — by anyone, in any register — by the states whose entitlements it secures. A pre-conference that defends 1.5°C rhetorically and leaves the certifying institution unmentioned would be the clearest possible confirmation that the fight has moved underneath the number.

watch.title: The climate panel's plenary and the timetable for the seventh assessment
watch.note: The panel meets in Addis Ababa from 12 to 16 October to settle whether its seventh assessment is completed in 2028, in time to inform the third global stocktake, or delivered in mid-2029. Reporting puts climate-vulnerable states on the 2028 side and India, Saudi Arabia, China, Russia and Kenya on the later one; that line-up is itself the first thing to verify, because it is currently carried by a newsletter rather than by any institutional source. The security consequence is specific and underappreciated: every legal and financial entitlement constructed in the last two years — the court's treatment of the panel as the best available science, the sea-level declaration's presumptions, the loss and damage fund's evidentiary practice — runs on assessment reports, and a year's delay in the assessment is a year's delay in all of it. A decision either way is a dated answer.

watch.title: Whether Somalia's rains arrive on the forecast and whether more money moves before they do
watch.note: The Deyr season runs October to December, the seasonal forecast was at essentially a hundred per cent probability of El Niño with 23 of 26 models projecting a very strong event, and between 2.5 and 3.5 million people are estimated exposed with about a million likely to be displaced. The anticipatory money identified so far is $7 million pre-approved from the central emergency response fund in June and £5 million from Britain on 24 September; the national humanitarian plan was at about a quarter funded. Two datable questions by early November: whether the Juba and Shabelle basins flood as forecast, and whether any further anticipatory allocation is announced before they do rather than after. This is the cleanest live test the field has of whether forecast-based financing works when every technical precondition is satisfied, and the answer arrives on a known schedule.
