active_trends.text: Removal of climate from security vehicles rather than only from language. Quiet this week on the American and Atlantic side and advanced on the European one, in a form the trend's original statement did not anticipate: the Union's own resilience instrument, due 28 October, is being built with the climate referent intact and, on the available evidence, without security of supply in it. The vehicle is not being emptied of climate; it is being emptied of security. Hold both halves together or the trend reads as an American peculiarity, which it no longer is.

US adaptation surviving only where reframed as disaster operations. No federal observable this week in either direction. At the level of the institute the reframing has stopped moving toward statehouses: no new state briefer in two weeks, and the only climate item in the window is a great-power scenario exercise on Arctic aerosol injection. That is a third register, not a deepening of the second.

Security Council shift from climate security to natural resource governance, and now past it. Greece's October programme carries no climate item in any framing, resource governance included, and the presidency named the succession as the month's business. Six consecutive weeks with nothing. The trend's useful form is now about what replaces climate rather than what it is renamed as: this month the Council gave its prime-ministerial slot to emerging technologies with a maritime emphasis.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments, complicated again and this time from the science side. The instrument question this week is not whether states will accept binding obligations but whether they will accept a binding reference body: Fiji's chief negotiator reports pressure to let scientific bodies other than the climate panel guide decisions, and the panel's own plenary from 12 October decides whether its next assessment lands in 2028 or 2029. An entitlement built on an assessment report is only as binding as the assessment's authority.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment — confirmed again and, more usefully, generalised. The defence climate strategy's €5 million structural line survived the budget and its action plan has still not appeared three months on: the money exists and the plan does not. And the pattern is no longer distinctively Dutch. The multilateral system's own climate-security unit has taken $18.27 million in nine years across fourteen governments. Read the trend as a property of this policy area rather than of the Dutch state.

Dutch public-opinion decline against the international average. Not refreshed this week; the evidence is now five months old and unchanged since the May survey. Recorded so the age of the evidence stays visible rather than the claim hardening by repetition.

Overshoot moving from a risk to a planning premise. Advanced sharply on the civilian planning side and in binding form: the European instrument due 28 October is reported to carry a 3°C reference scenario for Europe in its legislative proposal. A warming scenario written into law, rather than into guidance, is the furthest this has gone anywhere. On the other side of the ledger, Fiji is carrying 'hold the line on science and 1.5' into the pre-conference talks. The planning system and the negotiating system are now openly premised on different numbers.

High-mountain hazard migrating from the mode monitoring was built for to the mode it was not. Now a three-mode problem rather than two, and this week supplied the third. The August rock-ice cascade was too fast to warn against; this week's riverine flooding was warned against successfully, reaching about 980,000 people; the 304 landslides in between are forecastable in aggregate and not in particular, and that is where the deaths were. The cross-border half is unmoved: the China-India expert mechanism promised for September did not meet, and neither capital has answered Nepal's proposal.

The gap between what event attribution will certify and what climate finance is asked to pay for. Kept as a record of a frame this digest judged wrong in week five, and now worth one amendment. The frame was wrong about the loss and damage fund, where the binding constraint is the instrument's ceiling rather than the evidence. It is not wrong everywhere: in Europe this week the absence of a certified attribution and the absence of a public cost estimate left both the hazard and its price to a private damage function. Where there is no public number, a private one becomes the number.

Climate argued in whichever security register is locally unoccupied rather than in the field's own. Extended this week beyond security altogether. The energy agency's proposal that diversification costs be understood as a 'mineral security premium' converts a security argument into a priced insurance option, which is the first substitution in six weeks that leaves the security vocabulary behind rather than borrowing a different part of it. The Berlin convening's theme — security, freedom and prosperity — is the same operation in a diplomatic register. Insurance language is commensurable with budgets in a way threat language never was, and it prices out everything about the harm that cannot be priced.

The assets a changing hazard environment destroys are increasingly publicly indispensable and privately owned, with no instrument settling who pays. Advanced on the instrument side for the first time: the European framework due 28 October is expected to stand up a climate insurance alliance and to oblige the naming of risk owners for every major climate risk. That is the first serious attempt anywhere to assign the liability this trend is about. Watch who the named owners turn out to be, and whether the alliance's loss estimates come from the insurers who will price the cover.

The climate referent and the security register being decoupled, in both directions, by different actors in the same week. Sharpened into a clean pair this week. The alliance kept the hazards and dropped the word in September; the Union is keeping the word and, on the available evidence, dropping the supply-security content in October. Two European resilience instruments six weeks apart, one defining resilience as assured supply and the other as insured recovery, with nothing visible connecting them and no external-action or defence involvement found in the second.

The contest is moving from the hazard to the apparatus that measures and prices it. Three separate instances in one week: a joint appeal by two United Nations agencies to protect the radio-frequency bands weather and climate observation physically requires, ahead of the 2027 spectrum conference; a reported move among states to let scientific bodies other than the climate panel guide decisions, with the panel's own assessment timetable contested in parallel; and the only circulating figure for Europe's 2026 heat losses coming from a credit insurer's proprietary damage functions because no public institution has produced one. The common structure is that each is a fight over an input the field has treated as given. Watch for the fourth instance in the places this already touches: whose loss estimates the European insurance alliance adopts, and what evidentiary basis the loss and damage fund settles on.

open_threads.text: PSI's current funding phase. Unmoved and now unassessable by the route being used: the institute's own domain refused retrieval for a fourth consecutive week. The sister site opened as before and carries no funding information, only curated work by other institutions. The last publicly datable announcement of a funding phase remains December 2019, which is close to seven years without a public statement about the platform's resourcing. The thread stays open with the method flagged: four refusals is a hole in the observation, not a finding about the institute.

Whether NATO published a fourth Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. Still no, still no statement, and the question is now almost fully displaced by a better one. The alliance's own climate change and security centre of excellence is convening a defence-climate summit in Montréal on 15 and 16 October under the title 'Resilient Defence: Climate-Smart Investments on the Road to 5%', with nine thematic tracks and serving officers speaking. The climate work is plainly continuing inside the alliance structure; what has stopped is the instrument that produced a public, citable, annual judgement. Those are different losses and only the second is reversible by anyone outside the alliance.

Whether the International Military Council's World Climate and Security Report has formally lapsed. Re-checked for a fifth consecutive week: no report since the 2024 edition and the most recent item of any kind still the open letter of 23 October 2025. This week supplies the test the dormancy fails. That letter argued for clean energy investment inside the alliance's 1.5-per-cent non-core defence spending target; the alliance's own centre of excellence is now convening a summit on climate-smart defence investment on the road to 5 per cent. The council's position has become other people's agenda in the month it said nothing.
Funding trajectory of the joint United Nations climate security unit.
open_threads.resolution: Answered in magnitude, by a printed portfolio report rather than by the dashboard that has refused to render for three weeks. Cumulative deposits to the joint programme between 2016 and 2024 were $18.27 million, which places it thirteenth of fifteen funds in the trust fund office's climate and environment portfolio, against $808.89 million for the largest and about $2 million a year for this one. Fourteen governments contribute, eleven of them European; the Netherlands is not among them. The programme is not being wound down — a third phase runs 2026 to 2028 with ten advisers deployed — and it is funded at the level of a mid-sized national research grant. One consequence for this digest's own published record: Britain's £1 million of 25 September, reported here as three tenths of one per cent of a £331 million package and treated as a rounding error, is on the order of 5 per cent of everything this programme has ever received. The denominator was wrong. What remains unanswered is the year-by-year trajectory and whether the third phase has a stated requirement, which is carried forward as a separate question.

open_threads.text: Whether the 2028-2034 budget carries a security-tagged climate line. Not advanced, and the calendar now gives it a date: a special European Council on the next long-term budget is scheduled for 26 and 27 November, with the Commission's work programme for next year presented on 20 October. Nothing found this week on a security-tagged climate line in any of it. One thing to carry into November: the nearer instrument, the resilience framework of 28 October, is expected to arrive with an insurance alliance rather than a budget line, which would make insurance the Union's chosen financing route for climate risk and leave the budget question about something else.

Chinese defence doctrine on climate — gap, seventh week, and the negative observable has now hardened from a broken commitment into a missed deadline. China's own foreign ministry text of the 25 August boundary talks committed both sides to holding the next China-India expert-level mechanism meeting on trans-border rivers in September, with hydrological data sharing and the renewal of the relevant memoranda on the agenda. September has ended with no meeting found from either side. The doctrinal absence is unchanged; the procedural one is now dated and specific, which makes it the better instrument.

Any Indian security document on climate — gap, seventh week, and after seven weeks the instrument itself should be questioned. Indian climate statecraft is transacted through finance, trade and water by ministries that do not write security documents, so a security document may simply be the wrong place to look. Two better instruments are now identified and both are datable: India's position in the expert-level mechanism on trans-border rivers, and its reported resistance — with Saudi Arabia, China, Russia and Kenya — to completing the climate panel's seventh assessment by 2028 rather than mid-2029. The second is decided between 12 and 16 October and is the first thing to verify next week, since it currently rests on a newsletter.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: the reinsurer's own page would not open and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved on 17 September 2026, and the answer is not one of the two the thread was framed to expect. World Weather Attribution published *Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits*, with contributors in ten countries across glaciology, mountain hydrology, climate science, seismology, humanitarian practice and social science. It attributes the hazard environment and not the event: about 1.5°C added to July-August temperatures by human-caused climate change, about 2°C annually — larger than global mean warming — individual winter months as much as 3°C, and the 0°C isotherm rising roughly 100 metres a decade into the bedrock that failed. It states explicitly that it has not assessed whether this specific rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change, while asserting that warming at a rate beyond the global mean increases the likelihood and severity of such hazards. It then concludes that the event exceeded the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, that this constitutes a soft limit to adaptation given constrained habitable land and population increase, and that addressing loss and damage through recovery and reconstruction has become an unavoidable part of climate response. So: no event attribution, a hazard-environment attribution, and the policy conclusion reached through adaptation limits instead of causation. The successor question is the `adaptation-limits-adjudication` thread. Reporting figures that travelled with it: the debris flood ran 200 km in under seven hours at average speeds around 188 km/h and deposited 30.5 million cubic metres of material.

open_threads.text: What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its listed member organisations include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies including the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat. Stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named, and the site is labelled beta. Cite it as a consortium finding attributed to the consortium; do not upgrade it to institutional authority.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the loss and damage fund applies to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution. Unchanged and still demoted: the question was mis-framed, as the pushback in week five set out, because the binding constraint is the instrument's $20 million per-project ceiling rather than the evidence. No board movement this week, no emergency meeting, and the tenth board meeting is reported for December in Manila. The fund's own site has still not been opened by this routine; the route identified — board documents posted through the climate convention — has not yet been tried and should be.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of national output to at least 2 — survives into a government commitment, and whether the review's concession that some damage will not be prevented is adopted or dropped. Third weekly checkpoint, third week with no answer. No cabinet response to the 2027 delta programme was found three weeks after it was laid, and the one international climate item on the parliamentary floor on 1 October was a two-minute motions debate. One new consideration: the European framework of 28 October is expected to oblige the naming of risk owners for every major climate risk, which cuts directly across a Dutch model that distributes responsibility by design. If anything forces a Dutch answer it may be that rather than the ask itself.

Whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will now receive it. Unchanged on its own terms and newly interesting from an unexpected direction. No fund board, development bank or court reasoned from adaptation limits this week. But the European framework due 28 October is expected to require named risk owners for every major climate risk in key sectors, which would create, for the first time anywhere, an administrative forum in which the question 'was this risk beyond the limits of what could be adapted to' has an identified respondent. Administrative adjudication was not the route this thread was watching and may be the one that arrives first.

Who bears roughly Rs300 billion of privately held losses in Nepal, and whether a sovereign loss and damage claim can cover them. Unmoved on the instrument and worse on the arithmetic. This week's rain added at least 43 deaths, 227 houses destroyed, 142 damaged and 31 bridges damaged across Baglung, Manang, Myagdi and Mustang, almost none of it insured and most of it privately held. The maximum single-project claim on the fund remains $20 million against an assessed recovery bill of about $4.7 billion from the August event alone. Each week the numerator grows and the ceiling does not.

Whether any security institution reads the sea-level declaration as a security instrument. First answer, and it is the strongest available negative. Greece — a maritime state with the world's largest merchant fleet — took the Security Council presidency for October and gave its prime minister's signature slot to emerging technologies with a maritime emphasis, a week after the General Assembly settled by consensus that statehood and maritime entitlements survive the physical loss of territory. Not that nobody noticed: the institution with the competence, the opportunity and the national interest used its month on something else. The thread stays open because the declaration's security uptake could still come from a court, a navy or a boundary commission rather than from the Council.

Whether NATO's removal of the climate referent from its resilience baseline is a one-off drafting choice or standing practice. Nothing new from the alliance this week, and the next observable is dated: the Montréal summit of 15 and 16 October, convened by the alliance's own climate change and security centre of excellence, is titled around climate-smart investment and names climate in its own framing throughout. If the alliance's centre of excellence says climate freely while the alliance's binding requirements do not, the removal is a drafting discipline applied to instruments that bind rather than a change in what the alliance thinks — which is a narrower and more tractable finding than the one this thread was opened to test.
Whether money reaches Somalia before the October-to-December rains.
open_threads.resolution: Answered yes, in part, and the answer required correcting this digest. Money did move before the rains: $7 million was pre-approved from the central emergency response fund in June for flood response preparedness ahead of the El Niño, alongside $10 million for drought response, and on 24 September Britain announced £5 million specifically for Deyr flood preparedness, split equally between a health, nutrition, water and protection programme led by Action Against Hunger and a Shabelle-basin rehabilitation programme delivered through three agencies, expected to reach about 600,000 people. Last week's digest said the money had not come; it had, one day before that was written. The proportions still carry the original finding: about £5 million and $7 million of anticipatory money against 2.5 to 3.5 million people exposed, roughly a million expected to be displaced, and a humanitarian plan at about a quarter funded. What happens next — whether the forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss — is carried forward as a new question rather than as this one.

open_threads.text: Whether India or China responds to Nepal's proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, made from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September. Nothing from either capital by 4 October, and the week made the silence more expensive. Between 24 September and 1 October Nepal had 304 landslides, 87 floods, an avalanche at a Himlung Himal base camp and at least 43 deaths, with landslides damming rivers in Manang and Mustang and creating exactly the cross-border downstream risk the proposal's joint early-warning and data-sharing provisions address. In the same window the China-India expert mechanism that was committed to meeting in September did not meet. Two refusals of the same thing, by the two capitals the proposal names.

Whether the joint United Nations climate-security programme's third phase has a stated funding requirement, and whether contributions into it are rising, flat or falling. The magnitude question is closed at $18.27 million of cumulative deposits to 2024. The trajectory is not, and it is the one that says whether a programme funded at about $2 million a year is growing into its third phase or coasting. A figure of $52.4 million as the requirement since 2018 with $27.5 million mobilised by June 2025 circulates in secondary summaries and could not be confirmed against any institutional document; it is recorded here as unverified and should not be repeated until it is. The route is identified and not yet taken: the programme publishes a consolidated annual report and a consolidated financial report for each year, and the 2025 pair is listed.

Whether the climate panel remains the reference science for climate decisions, on what timetable, and which states are pressing on each axis. Fiji's chief negotiator says some countries want scientific bodies other than the panel to guide decisions, and objects on participation grounds: small states have no national research agency of comparable scale, so a shift of reference body excludes them from the decisions it informs. In parallel the panel's plenary from 12 to 16 October decides whether its seventh assessment is completed for 2028, in time to inform the third global stocktake, or delivered in mid-2029. Reporting places India, Saudi Arabia, China, Russia and Kenya on the later side; that line-up rests on a newsletter and is the first thing to verify. Why it is a security question: the court's 2025 treatment of the panel's reports as the best available science, the sea-level declaration's presumptions and the loss and damage fund's evidentiary practice all run on assessment reports, so both the identity of the assessing body and the date of the next assessment are load-bearing for entitlements that already exist.

Whether any security institution treats the meteorological observing system's radio spectrum as an asset to be defended before the 2027 radiocommunication conference. The telecommunications union and the meteorological organization escalated to a joint appeal by both Secretaries-General on 28 September, framed as public safety, naming satellite sounding, weather radar, lightning location and hydrological monitoring as dependent on bands fixed by atmospheric physics rather than by choice. Military meteorology runs on the same bands and allied early warning on the same satellites, and nothing from any defence ministry, alliance body or national security council was found engaging it. Two things to establish: how much protected meteorological spectrum is actually under live reallocation pressure on the conference agenda, which no public figure yet gives, and which way European administrations resolve the conflict between their meteorological services and their spectrum auctions in the coordinated negotiating position.

Whether any public institution produces an estimate of what Europe's 2026 heat season cost, to set against the private one. The only figure in circulation is an insurer's: about €113 billion of annual output across 30 countries, 0.46 per cent of combined projected output, from proprietary damage functions applied to each country's most intense five-day episode. It is not peer-reviewed, not replicable from the public record, and produced by a firm that sells cover against the risk. It will be the number in European policy documents for a year unless something else appears. The institutions that could produce one hold the inputs — the statistical office, the environment agency, the national meteorological services — and none has converted exposure and mortality data into a growth figure. The question has a date attached: if the framework of 28 October stands up a climate insurance alliance without specifying an independent basis for loss estimation, the private number becomes the official one by default.

Whether the Somali Deyr forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss. The conditions are as favourable as forecast-based financing ever gets: a seasonal forecast at essentially a hundred per cent probability of El Niño with 23 of 26 models projecting a very strong event, named basins in the Juba and Shabelle, specified measures, months of lead time, and about $7 million plus £5 million committed in advance. Against that, 2.5 to 3.5 million people exposed, about a million expected to be displaced, and a humanitarian plan at roughly a quarter funded. Two datable questions by early November: whether the basins flood as forecast, and whether any further anticipatory allocation is announced before they do rather than after. The field has no cleaner test of whether its central operational doctrine works when every technical precondition is met.

Whether any candidate for Secretary-General states a position on climate, and in particular on Security Council competence over it. The presidency for October named agreement on the succession as the month's business, with several straw polls planned; the fourth was held on 29 September with seven candidates, and reporting gives the leading candidate at ten encourage, three discourage and two no opinion, with the Council not yet moved to colour-coded ballots. Nothing was found on the climate positions of any of the seven, from the Council, from the Assembly's dialogues or from the candidates' own material. The institution that houses the field's only standing climate-security machinery — at $18.27 million over nine years — may have a new head within weeks, and the vetoed 2021 draft resolution means Council competence over climate is a live question a new Secretary-General would inherit. The field has not asked a single candidate about it in public.

open_moves.text: Denmark's Security Council food-security debate, outcome document unconfirmed. Unchanged, and October closes one route: Greece's programme of work carries no food-security item either, so there is no Council occasion this month on which an outcome document could surface. Where food security did go institutionally remains the alliance's fourth baseline requirement of 15 September, which obliges allies to hold exercised contingency plans to secure food and water supply during crisis and conflict — a binding instrument where a Council outcome document would have been a statement.

The American climate-security institute's philanthropic-funding bet. Advanced on register for the second consecutive week, and this time in a direction the thread did not anticipate. Its only climate item between 28 September and 4 October is the announcement, on 2 October, of a private tabletop exercise with a solar-geoengineering research organisation on the security dynamics of a fictional 2030 stratospheric aerosol injection deployment in the Arctic (D2). Three registers in three weeks — statehouse briefers, an alliance-requirements analysis, now a great-power geoengineering scenario — which reads less like a repositioning than like an institute placing several bets at once. Still nothing on the money.

The Abyei climate, peace and security report and the next peacekeeping mandate renewal. Unchanged. The Stockholm institute's climate-change-and-security publications list still ends at the August study and shows nothing for September or October, and the Lake Chad fact sheet listed earlier remains unread by this routine. Under the split rule this is lead time rather than a finding. One calendar note: the Council holds a seminar and consultative meeting with the African Union on 21 to 23 October, which is the nearest occasion on which the Abyei file could surface in the security register.
PIF security-declaration merger.

The European integrated framework for climate resilience. Substantially advanced and now the most consequential dated instrument in this digest. Presentation is fixed for 28 October as a package of a communication, a legislative proposal, a recommendation to public and private sectors and a Commission decision. Announced contents: Europe's hundred most vulnerable territories identified, a 3°C reference scenario for Europe in the legislative proposal, a duty on the Union and member states to assign named risk owners for every major climate risk in key sectors, a climate insurance alliance and a European heatwave plan. The Environment Council sits on 12 October and the Energy Council on 29 October. One contested point worth holding: a specialist policy service's headline says security of supply goes unmentioned in it, and the body of that report could not be read. The 20 October date this digest carried for three weeks was wrong — that is the day the Commission presents next year's work programme, a different document.

Succession to the Secretary-General. Advanced and now on a declared timetable. A fourth straw poll was held on 29 September with seven candidates, Michelle Bachelet having withdrawn on 20 September; the Council did not release results, and reporting gives Rebeca Grynspan at ten encourage, three discourage and two no opinion, an improvement of one and two respectively on the third poll, with Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett at eight and six. The Council has not moved to colour-coded ballots, so whether the discouragement sits with a permanent member is unknown. Greece's presidency named October as the month to make progress on or even agree the appointment, with several polls planned. For this field the open question is not who wins but that nobody has asked any of the seven a public question about climate or about Council competence over it.

The November conference of the parties at Antalya, 9 to 20 November, under a Türkiye-Australia presidency with the Turkish environment and urbanisation minister Murat Kurum as president-designate and the Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as president of negotiations. Advanced on substance and on personnel. The presidency launched two pledges from United Nations headquarters on 21 September: a global electrification pledge to raise electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 with a building energy-intensity cut of at least 25 per cent, and an Antalya artificial-intelligence pledge developed with the telecommunications union. Note the coincidence of institutions: the same union that is party to the conference presidency's technology pledge is the forum in which meteorological spectrum will be contested in 2027 (B2). The pre-conference talks of 5 to 8 October are where the agenda narrows.

Whether overshoot is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. Advanced decisively, and not by a security institution. The European legislative proposal due 28 October is reported to carry a 3°C reference scenario for Europe, which would put a warming premise into binding law rather than into planning guidance — further than the environment programme's own report went. Security institutions remain outside it: nothing from any defence ministry or alliance body on overshoot this week. The counter-move is now explicit on the negotiating side, with Fiji carrying 'hold the line on science and 1.5' into the pre-conference talks.

Whether the small island states' legal-character defence of 1.5°C holds through the Assembly session and the November conference. Advanced, and the defence has changed shape in a way worth recording. The argument being carried into the pre-conference talks by Fiji's chief negotiator is not about the number's legal character at all: it is a procedural defence of the climate panel as the reference body, on the ground that substituting other scientific bodies excludes states with no national research agency of comparable scale. Defending the certifier rather than the threshold is a stronger position for small states, because participation is a claim they can win where accuracy is one they cannot. Method note: the alliance's own pages were not tried this week, so this rests on Fiji's statements and on its climate minister, who chairs the Pacific small island developing states.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data wall. No movement on funding and a bad week for the data wall: the China-India expert mechanism committed to meeting in September did not meet, and neither India nor China has answered Nepal's proposal for the three-country mechanism that would formalise the sharing. What this week did establish, unhelpfully, is that the hazard class that killed people in Nepal between 24 September and 1 October was landslide rather than glacial lake outburst, and a glacier-hazard early-warning programme would not have reached any of them.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. Superseded in practice. Nepal's posture is now unambiguously outward and institutional rather than defensive: a prime ministerial proposal for a trilateral mechanism, a public description of the existing financing instruments as grossly inadequate, and a continuing reconstruction-finance circuit through lenders. The inward-facing question about assistance limits has not recurred and should be closed next week unless something revives it.

Whether the climate convention secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any European security institution adopts the formulation.
open_moves.resolution: Answered on both halves and not in the way the question expected. A European security institution did adopt a security framing: on 24 September the Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks. But it adopted this field's own formulation, national security risk, not the secretariat's economic-security substitution. And the secretary himself substituted again in the same week, telling Climate Week that electrification shields countries, families and businesses from fossil-fuel supply shocks and calling it a development strategy, an industrial strategy, a health strategy and a security strategy — security fourth, and meaning supply security. So the two moved past each other: the institution reached for the field's register in the same week the secretariat reached past it. The question is closed because its premise has been falsified. It assumed the secretariat's phrasing would be the vector by which the security frame travelled into European institutions, and the frame travelled without it.

open_moves.text: Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent ask converts into any government commitment. Third checkpoint passed with silence. No cabinet response to the 2027 programme was found three weeks after it was laid, against one day in 2025, and the parliamentary week produced a steel-slag discussion and a rail-freight debate in the responsible committee and nothing on water. The nearest thing to pressure now comes from outside: the European framework of 28 October is expected to require named risk owners, which is awkward for a governance model built on distributed responsibility.

Whether Nepal's reconstruction bill produces a loss and damage response, and on what evidentiary basis. Unmoved and arithmetically worse. No board movement, no emergency meeting, and the tenth board meeting reported for December in Manila. Meanwhile the bill grew: at least 43 further deaths, 227 houses destroyed and 31 bridges damaged between 24 September and 1 October. The claim remains at the instrument's $20 million per-project ceiling against about $4.7 billion assessed for the August event alone. The fund's own site has still not opened for this routine and the alternative route — board documents posted through the climate convention — has not been tried.
Whether the rescission was announced as expected, whether the endangerment-finding proposal followed, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate.
open_moves.resolution: All three answered. The partial repeal of the carbon pollution standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants was finalised on 14 September 2026 by Administrator Lee Zeldin, signed at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston rather than on its sidelines; the agency prices it at $310 billion in savings and calls it the largest power-sector deregulatory action in US history. The separate proposal followed simultaneously: EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse-gas standard for the sector, the vehicle for repealing the power-plant endangerment finding, with $370 million in claimed direct compliance-cost savings. And the ministerial's outcome document, a Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué, does not mention climate: it grounds critical minerals in energy security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies and economic development, and calls for voluntary and collaborative cooperation respecting national sovereignty and 'different domestic pathways'. Canada's own readout of the meeting likewise contains no reference to climate change. Environmental organisations have said they will litigate. The substitution this digest read off the ministerial's branding last week is confirmed in a negotiated multilateral text, which is why this closes as landed rather than as too early.

open_moves.text: Whether NATO ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual climate and security assessment. Still no statement, and the displacement is now visible from two directions at once. The binding instrument revised on 15 September carries the hazards without the word; the alliance's own climate change and security centre of excellence is convening a summit on 15 and 16 October that carries the word throughout. The assessment series — the one public, citable, annual judgement the alliance produced — is the only thing that has actually stopped.

Whether the relocation of the evidentiary question from causation to adaptation limits is taken up by the institutions that have to apply it. No fund board, bank or court reasoned from adaptation limits this week. One new route, from an unexpected direction: the European framework due 28 October is expected to require named risk owners for every major climate risk, which would create an administrative respondent to the question of whether a given loss was beyond the limits of feasible adaptation. The attribution network has published nothing since 17 September, including nothing on this week's Nepali landslides or on Europe's heat season.

Whether the American climate-security field's move to the state level is a durable relocation or a holding pattern. Second consecutive week of counter-evidence, and stronger than the first. No new state briefer has appeared since the Ohio one of 18 September, and the institute's only climate item in this window is an Arctic geoengineering tabletop (D2) — international, speculative and unminuted, which is about as far from a statehouse readership as the field goes. On the evidence so far the statehouse series looks like one of several simultaneous bets rather than a relocation. No state government has yet been named as commissioner or partner on any of the five briefers, and no second American institute has started writing for statehouses.

Whether the asymmetry in the Dutch budget — flood defence funded, spatial adaptation and freshwater reduced over the longer term — survives the cabinet's response to the 2027 delta programme and the autumn estimates, or is corrected by amendment. No amendment found and no cabinet response found. The parliamentary budget rounds on infrastructure and water fall later in the autumn, so this is lead time rather than an answer. The defence side of the same pattern hardened: the €5 million structural climate-security line stands and the action plan that would spend it has still not appeared three months after it was promised.

The British, European and Kenyan foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, 24 September. Five weeks on, no institutional follow-through has appeared from any of the three. The commitments were to horizon scanning inside national and regional security systems and to joint risk assessment; the Council's October programme, which is where a European-led climate item would have shown, carries none, and nothing was found from the Union's external action service. One partial exception on the British side, and it is money rather than machinery: £5 million for Somali flood preparedness announced on 24 September, the same day as the dialogue.

Britain's £331 million for climate-driven instability, of which £330 million to the Global Environment Facility and £1 million to the joint United Nations climate security unit. Recalibrated, and this digest's reading of it was wrong in a way worth stating. The £1 million was reported here as three tenths of one per cent of the package and treated as a rounding error. Measured against the recipient rather than against the package, it is on the order of 5 per cent of all the money that programme has received since 2016. The denominator was the error. Britain's September total is also larger than reported here: £5 million for Somali flood preparedness was announced on 24 September, separately from the package. The open question stands — whether the proportion is a one-off or the going rate — but it is now a question about a programme that has only ever had $18.27 million, which is a different question.

Nepal's proposal, from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September, for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China, to share satellite data, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, run joint early warning and coordinate cross-border relief. No response from either capital by 4 October, and the cost of the silence rose. Between 24 September and 1 October Nepal recorded 304 landslides and 87 floods with at least 43 deaths, and landslides dammed rivers in Manang and Mustang, creating precisely the cross-border downstream risk the proposal's data-sharing and joint-warning provisions address. In the same window the China-India expert mechanism committed to meeting in September did not meet. Two refusals of the same thing, in the same month, by the two capitals the proposal names.

NATO's revision and first public release of its seven baseline requirements for resilience, 15 September. Nothing new from the alliance this week. The next dated observable is the Montréal summit of 15 and 16 October, convened by the alliance's own climate change and security centre of excellence with a Canadian defence association, titled around climate-smart investment on the road to 5 per cent and running nine tracks including procurement resilience metrics, climate intelligence in planning and critical-minerals supply chains. If the centre of excellence names climate freely while the binding requirements do not, the removal was a drafting discipline for instruments that bind rather than a change of mind — a narrower finding, and a testable one.

Australia's Climate Week keynote on climate security as national security, 21 September, and the immediate challenge to it from a former Australian chief of defence asking where the plan is. No answer from Canberra this week. The near-term test is institutional rather than rhetorical: the Australian climate minister presides over negotiations for the November conference and opened the pre-conference talks in Fiji on 5 October, with the Pacific agenda built on 1.5°C, finance access and oceans. Whether any security content appears in what he presides over, as against what he says in a keynote, is answerable by 8 October.

Fiji's four-pillar position for the pre-conference talks, set out on 29 September by its permanent secretary for environment and climate change and chief negotiator: hold the line on science and 1.5°C, climate finance, oceans, and Pacific leadership. Open on the first pillar in its specific form. The defence is procedural rather than substantive — the objection to substituting other scientific bodies for the climate panel is that small states have no national research agency of comparable scale and would be excluded from the decisions those bodies inform. Resolves, partly, at the close of the talks on 8 October: whether the outcome text or chair's summary names the panel as the reference science, and whether the ocean pillar acquires a named deliverable for Antalya. Resolves more fully at the panel's plenary from 12 October.

The American climate-security institute's private tabletop exercise with a solar-geoengineering research organisation on the security dynamics of a fictional 2030 stratospheric aerosol injection deployment to slow Arctic warming, announced 2 October for 14 October alongside the Montréal defence-climate summit, by registration and with no participants named. Open on three things, none of which the format is designed to answer: whether anything citable comes out of it, whether any state or alliance body takes part, and whether the exercise surfaces risks or normalises the premise. The last is the one that matters and the opacity is itself the finding — the field's most consequential emerging question is being worked in a room with no minutes. Watch for any acknowledgement after 16 October.

Greece's Security Council programme of work for October, announced 1 October: signature events on children and armed conflict (26 October) and on emerging technologies with a maritime emphasis (29 October), a seminar and consultative meeting with the African Union (21 to 23 October), and no climate item in any framing. The presidency named agreement on the Secretary-General as the month's substantive business. Recorded as a move because a presidency's programme is one of the few genuinely discretionary acts in the institution, and because a maritime state declined to pick up the sea-level declaration adopted by consensus a week earlier. Resolves on 31 October: whether any climate or sea-level content reaches the Council in any format, including under the African Union item or in a signature-event concept note.

The Berlin climate and security conference of 6 October 2026, hosted by the German foreign ministry with the institute that founded it in 2019, under the theme 'A climate for security, freedom and prosperity', in person by invitation and streamed, with stated objectives including the demonstration that national and human security must be considered together. Open on whether anything with a named owner comes out of it: the conference has no standing output document, which is why six previous editions have produced influence impossible to trace. The theme's three nouns are themselves a datum — a foreign ministry arguing climate inside a coalition that does not lead with climate. Recorded here with the correction it forces: this digest concluded for three weeks that there was no 2026 edition, and the reasoning that produced that is in the pushback.
